framing: A retrieved rule still has to make the cut
paragraphs: Search has found the right passage. It sits at rank three, and the generator has room for two. The rule is in your candidate list, your candidate recall is happy, but the rule still has no way to influence the answer. A more careful scoring pass can change that.

A new case isolates the problem. A service account needs the legacy token rule, AUTH-14, while troubleshooting, password-reset, and audit-export passages compete for the same space. These records follow the same permission and tracing rules as before, with their own source IDs.

We follow the same four candidates through a hand-written scorer, and then through a real cross-encoder. Reading the question and passage together gives a model a chance to tell actors, actions, and conditions apart. You still have to know what text got scored and how a score becomes a place in the prompt.

Ordering metrics then show whether the rule crossed the line that matters. The counterexamples separate that gain from missing candidates, cut-off conditions, wrong decisions, and slow requests, which prepares you to measure what the generator actually says.
outcomes: Explain joint question and passage scoring, and the limit candidate depth places on it.
Keep source identity and the scored text intact through reranking and packing.
Measure ordering gains at your context budget, separately from answer correctness.
question: What changed when the right passage moved into context, and what do you still not know about the answer?
